# Performance verdict: BLOCK, round 1

Subject: pr:315

## R315-P1: the non-dry sweep still decodes the whole roster for receipt.after

crates/daemon/src/reaper.rs:290-297 still calls
registry.list(SeatFilter::default()), then filters tombstoned_at in Rust.
crates/daemon/src/death_sweep.rs:93-101 calls this with dry_run=false every
5,000 ms by default (death_sweep.rs:18). The initial read is fixed, but the
final read is not: each sweep materializes L+T rows, previously 2T, not only
live rows. At the supplied copied fleet size that is 3,467 rather than
6,524 descriptors per sweep; T=3,262 and L=205. History still determines
one full-roster scan/decoding pass every five seconds, even when nothing dies.

Independent copy timings confirm the residual: the final query at this head
still returns 3,262 rows and costs 6.2495 ms median CPU. The advertised
6.26 -> 0.34 ms covers only the initial list, not the entire sweep. The
two-list SQL/tuple-materialization proxy is about 12.754 -> 6.5915 ms;
these sums of query medians are not a measured complete Rust sweep.

Fix this directly coupled call in round 2: use the same live-only filter
and take len(). It preserves the freshly observed live count, including
rows registered/revived/retired during the sweep, without decoding retired
history. Existing receipt semantics and mutation CAS need not change.
Correct the cost row to price both reads. The author has acknowledged the
miss and is preparing this change; that does not alter this head's verdict.
This is the sole blocking finding, not a demand for a new abstraction,
profiler, exhaustive mutation inventory, or archiving policy.

## Verified cost and query properties

The observer is one live registry list per daemon per 600 ms by default
(1.667/s, not one query per seat); its subsequent pane work still scales
with tracked panes. Source: pane_observer.rs:227-244 and core/config.rs:209.
The live list now visits L index entries and materializes its matching live
rows, not T historical entries. On the identical 3,262/205 copy, median CPU
was 0.847 -> 0.345 ms; the reaper's initial read was 6.377 -> 0.342 ms.
These independently reproduce the author's 0.84 -> 0.34 and 6.26 -> 0.34
query results. No deployed daemon CPU saving is established by this copy.

The exact Rust SQL constants were extracted from registry.rs; 45 harness/
folder/parent filter combinations and pane+live cases produced identical
rows and order. EXPLAIN uses seats_live without a temp sort, and sqlite_stat1
reports "205 1". The partial index occupied 3 pages/12,288 bytes. Dropping
it made the indexed live query refuse with "no such index: seats_live".
The pane branch remains first, so its narrower candidate seek wins when
both filters are present; its existing matching-row ORDER BY sort remains.

There is no new loop, timer, poll cadence, per-seat process launch, or launch
site in this diff: steady-state launch delta is zero by code inspection.
Existing liveness probes, per-live-row refreshes and mutation checks remain.
The migration is additive, not destructive, and adds no retention policy.
The reaper's existing process/pane eligibility decides retirement; unknown
evidence and pane-presence checks remain one-directional BRAKES. The list
filter does not introduce an age policy or authorize a new mutation.

## Index write and migration cost

One live insertion adds an index entry; tombstoning removes it; revival adds
it back. A normal registry upsert explicitly assigns tombstoned_at even
unchanged, so a live->live update deletes/reinserts seats_live's entry. The
cost row should include updates, not just initial register/tombstone.
State/seq-only activity updates do not maintain seats_live: verified with
EXPLAIN bytecode, not inferred from the presence of a WHERE predicate.

Paired alternating batches (200 x 50 statements per variant, CPU median):
live upsert 4.58 -> 4.92 us/statement (+0.34); live tombstone 1.88 -> 2.08
(+0.20); state-only 1.60 -> 1.60. Insert 3.62 -> 3.46 was a small unfavorable
measurement for the baseline, not evidence that an added index speeds inserts.
Bytecode confirms the extra relevant index operations. These in-memory
statement measurements exclude commit/fsync, event publication, sqlx and
Rust descriptor decoding, so do not represent end-to-end write latency.

Migration 0049 built the index on the private 3,262-row copy in 0.471 ms CPU/
1.356 ms wall. It is a one-time seats-table read plus index construction,
not a full-store archive or a steady-state scan. This small-copy result is
not a large-DB startup latency bound. SQLx's migration ledger supplies
normal reopen idempotence; manually replaying bare CREATE INDEX is not
idempotent. An older v48 binary refuses a v49 store by the existing
found > SCHEMA_VERSION guard (migrate.rs:174-184); it does not silently
operate through the new version. This is the repository's existing contract.
